plan: Ten new items, each topic searched in all three verbal banks first (a songbird-pitch inference was dropped because SAT 027 already uses that study): qualified/malleable WIC, earthworm structure, tree-ring inference, garden per-plot data, participle modifier, title agreement, 'For instance', cavefish location synthesis, Rossetti quotation.

passages.title: A trial semester
passages.text: When the school board reviewed the proposal to keep the public library open until 9 p.m., its response was ______: members praised the plan's goals but voted to fund only a one-semester trial before committing to a permanent change.

passages.title: Beaten thin
passages.text: Gold is unusually ______: a single gram of it can be hammered into a sheet nearly one square meter in area without tearing, a property that has made gold leaf a favorite of artists and bookbinders for centuries.

passages.title: Worms that came later
passages.text: For much of the twentieth century, many gardeners and naturalists in the northern United States and Canada assumed that the earthworms in local forests had always lived there. Studies of species and their histories, however, indicate that most earthworms in these northern forests arrived from Europe and Asia in soil and plants carried by settlers, because the glaciers of the last ice age had largely wiped out native earthworms in the region. Ecologists now study how these newcomers alter the leaf litter and soil of forests that developed without them.

passages.title: Narrow rings
passages.text: Researchers examining tree rings in a mountain valley found that pines on dry, south-facing slopes formed unusually narrow rings for an entire decade in the 1800s. Pines of the same species growing beside the valley's river, where groundwater is always available, formed rings of normal width during the same decade. These findings suggest that the narrow rings most likely reflect ______

passages.title: Three gardens
passages.text:
A city tracked three community gardens during one growing season.
Garden | Number of plots | Total harvest (kg)
A | 40 | 2,000
B | 25 | 1,500
C | 15 | 1,050
A city report claims that Garden C was the most productive per plot even though it had the fewest plots.

passages.title: A farmer's find
passages.text: The silver coins, ______ in 1903 by a farmer plowing a field near the river, are now displayed at the county museum alongside the farmer's own account of the discovery.

passages.title: Three generations
passages.text: Marisol Vega's 2015 novel The Orchards ______ the story of three generations of a family who run a fruit farm in central California, moving back and forth among their perspectives.

passages.title: Listening plants
passages.text: Some plants appear to respond to the sounds made by the insects that eat them. ______ in one experiment, thale cress plants that had been exposed to recordings of caterpillars chewing produced more of a defensive chemical when caterpillars later fed on them than plants that had been kept in silence did.

passages.title: A fish without eyes
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The Ozark cavefish is a small, pale fish with no functional eyes.
• It lives in caves and underground streams.
• Its range is limited to parts of Missouri, Arkansas, and Oklahoma.
• It is listed as threatened under the US Endangered Species Act.

passages.title: Who has seen the wind?
passages.text: "Who Has Seen the Wind?" is an 1872 poem by Christina Rossetti. In the poem, the speaker suggests that the wind itself cannot be seen and can be known only through its effects on other things.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: members praised the plan's goals but voted to fund only a one-semester trial
candidates.explanation: Praise combined with limited, conditional support is a "qualified" response: approval with reservations.

A.rationale: The board funded only a trial, which is more cautious than enthusiastic.

C.rationale: The board praised the goals and funded a trial, so it did not dismiss the plan.

D.rationale: The board took a clear position, praising the goals and voting on funding.

hints: Did the board fully support the plan, reject it, or something in between?
candidates.remember: Match the word to both halves of the explanation.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: can be hammered into a sheet nearly one square meter in area without tearing
candidates.explanation: A metal that can be hammered very thin without tearing is "malleable."

A.rationale: A brittle material breaks when struck, the opposite of what is described.

B.rationale: "Volatile" means unstable or quick to evaporate, which is unrelated to hammering.

D.rationale: "Abundant" means plentiful; the text is about how gold behaves when hammered, not how much exists.

hints: What happens to gold when it is hammered?
candidates.remember: The colon's explanation defines the missing word.

candidates.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It presents a long-held belief, evidence against it, and the research that followed.
choices.B: It compares two scientific theories and concludes that neither one can be tested.
choices.C: It describes an environmental problem and then recommends a practical solution.
choices.D: It traces a species from its origin in Europe to its extinction in North America.

candidates.evidence: assumed that the earthworms in local forests had always lived there
candidates.explanation: The text opens with an assumption (earthworms were native), presents evidence that they were introduced, and ends with current research on their effects.

B.rationale: The text does not present two theories or say anything is untestable.

C.rationale: No solution is recommended; ecologists are studying the effects.

D.rationale: The text concerns many species, and none is described as going extinct in North America.

hints: What does the word "however" signal in the second sentence?

strategy.explanation: Label each sentence's job, then match.

candidates.remember: Structure answers describe the job of each part in order.

candidates.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: a decade of unusually cold weather that slowed the growth of every tree in the valley.
choices.B: a disease that spread among trees growing along the river.
choices.C: the slope trees being much younger than the trees beside the river.
choices.D: a shortage of rainfall, since trees with a steady water supply grew normally.

candidates.evidence: where groundwater is always available, formed rings of normal width
candidates.explanation: Only the trees without a reliable water source grew poorly, which points to a lack of rain rather than a valley-wide cause such as cold.

A.rationale: Cold affecting every tree would have narrowed the riverside trees' rings too.

B.rationale: The riverside trees grew normally, so this has the pattern backward.

C.rationale: Nothing in the text concerns the trees' ages.

hints: What do the riverside trees have that the slope trees lack?

strategy.explanation: Rule out causes that would have affected both groups.

candidates.remember: A control group that was unaffected rules out shared causes.

candidates.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the report's claim?

choices.A: Garden A had the largest total harvest of the three gardens, with 2,000 kg in all.
choices.B: Garden C had only 15 plots but harvested 70 kg per plot, more than A (50 kg) or B (60 kg).
choices.C: Garden C harvested a total of 1,050 kg of produce during the growing season.
choices.D: Garden B had 25 plots, which is 10 more plots than Garden C had.

candidates.evidence: was the most productive per plot even though it had the fewest plots
candidates.explanation: The claim has two parts: C had the fewest plots and the highest harvest per plot. Only B supports both: 15 plots and 70 kg per plot versus 50 and 60.

A.rationale: Total harvest does not show productivity per plot.

C.rationale: A single total does not show either part of the claim.

D.rationale: This addresses plot counts but not productivity per plot.

hints: What two things does the claim say about Garden C?

strategy.explanation: Compute harvest per plot for each garden.

candidates.remember: Support every part of a two-part claim.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: are now displayed at the county museum
candidates.explanation: The sentence's main verb is "are displayed." The phrase between the commas must modify "coins," so it needs the participle "discovered," not a finite verb.

A.rationale: Adding the verb "were" creates a second main verb inside a phrase set off by commas.

B.rationale: This also adds a main verb inside the comma-enclosed phrase.

D.rationale: This inserts a full clause between the subject and its verb without a conjunction.

hints: What is the main verb of the sentence?

strategy.explanation: Find the main verb, then check what the phrase between commas must be.

candidates.remember: A phrase set off by commas cannot contain a second main verb.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.explanation: The subject is "novel," a single book whose title happens to be plural ("The Orchards"), so the singular "tells" is correct.

A.rationale: The subject is the novel, a single work, so the verb must be singular.

B.rationale: "Are" is plural and does not agree with the singular subject.

C.rationale: "Have" is plural and does not agree with the singular subject.

hints: Is the subject one thing or many?

strategy.explanation: Find the subject, ignoring the plural-looking title.

candidates.remember: A title names one work, so it takes a singular verb.

candidates.stem: The student wants to specify where the Ozark cavefish can be found. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: The Ozark cavefish, a small and pale fish, has no functional eyes and is rarely seen by people.
choices.B: The Ozark cavefish is listed as a threatened species under the US Endangered Species Act.
choices.C: The Ozark cavefish lives in caves and underground streams in parts of Missouri, Arkansas, and Oklahoma.
choices.D: Small and pale, the threatened Ozark cavefish has no functional eyes, unlike most other fish.

candidates.evidence: Its range is limited to parts of Missouri, Arkansas, and Oklahoma.
candidates.explanation: Only C names both the habitat (caves and underground streams) and the states where the fish lives.

A.rationale: This describes the fish's appearance, not where it lives.

B.rationale: This gives its legal status, not its location.

D.rationale: This combines appearance and status but gives no location.

hints: Which notes are about where the fish lives?

strategy.explanation: Match the choice to the stated goal.

candidates.remember: Rhetorical synthesis: choose the option that does exactly what the goal asks.

withdrawn.reason: withdrawn before review: solver B noted the thale cress study played back chewing vibrations through the leaf, not airborne sound; the passage's 'sounds' and 'recordings' wording is inaccurate. Resubmit with corrected wording in the next SAT batch.

item.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
item.evidence: Some plants appear to respond to the sounds
item.explanation: The second sentence gives a specific case of the general claim in the first, so "For instance" fits.

B.rationale: The experiment supports the first sentence rather than contrasting with it.

C.rationale: "Nevertheless" signals something that happens despite the previous point.

D.rationale: Nothing in the second sentence contrasts with the first.

hints: Is the second sentence an example, a contrast, or a result?
item.remember: Specific cases of a general claim take "for instance."

withdrawn.reason: withdrawn before review: solver B judged choice D ('Who has seen the wind? / Neither I nor you:') partly defensible because it illustrates the 'cannot be seen' half of the claim. Resubmit with the claim focused on knowing the wind through its effects.

item.stem: Which quotation from the poem most effectively illustrates the claim?

choices.B: "But when the leaves hang trembling, / The wind is passing through."
choices.D: "Who has seen the wind? / Neither I nor you:"

item.evidence: can be known only through its effects on other things
item.explanation: The trembling leaves are an effect that reveals the wind's presence, illustrating both parts of the claim.

A.rationale: The question alone does not show how the wind can be known.

C.rationale: This says no one has seen the wind but not how it can be known.

D.rationale: This shows that the wind is unseen but not that it is known through its effects.

hints: Which line shows something the wind does to something else?

strategy.explanation: The claim has two parts: unseen, and known by effects.

item.remember: A quotation must illustrate the whole claim, not just part of it.
